summaries.headline: Math Lacks Science of Reading's Clear Research Consensus
summaries.summary: Math achievement has stagnated for over a decade while reading instruction has gained momentum through the science of reading movement, leaving curriculum designers searching for equivalent research clarity in mathematics. Larry Berger, CEO of Amplify and creator of curricula used by nearly 20 million students, argues that math instruction still lacks the unified research base that has driven recent literacy reforms. The absence of this consensus leaves districts without clear guidance on effective math pedagogy, potentially explaining why mathematical progress has lagged behind reading gains in many schools.

summaries.headline: Google Pushes Enterprise AI Tools Into Education Market
summaries.summary: Google Cloud is rolling out new AI capabilities from its developer conference to enterprise customers, including school districts using Gemini Enterprise and Workspace tools. The updates include Gemini 3.5 Flash for complex workflows, Gemini Omni for video generation, and Spark agents that can automate multi-step tasks across Google Workspace and third-party systems like Microsoft SharePoint and ServiceNow. Districts already invested in Google's ecosystem gain access to more sophisticated AI automation without switching platforms, while competitors face pressure to match Google's integrated approach to enterprise AI deployment.

summaries.headline: Math Teachers Bridge Execution-Understanding Gap Using Hybrid Approaches
summaries.summary: Math teachers face a persistent challenge where students can solve complex equations but struggle to explain their reasoning, according to an educator with 30 years of experience teaching in both Italian and U.S. schools. The instructor found success combining structured, sequential concept-building from Italian pedagogy with real-world applications emphasized in American classrooms, explicitly connecting new material to prior knowledge through prompts like "What do we already know that can help us here?" This hybrid approach suggests that improving math instruction requires drawing from multiple teaching traditions rather than adhering to a single pedagogical model.

summaries.headline: Albany Extends Mamdani's School Control Through 2028
summaries.summary: New York state lawmakers agreed to extend Mayor Zohran Mamdani's control over the nation's largest school system through June 2028, alongside $143 million in additional funding for homeless students, foster children, and English language learners. The two-year extension falls short of the four-year timeline Mamdani and Governor Kathy Hochul requested and notably includes no governance reforms that might dilute mayoral authority—a departure from previous extensions that added parent representatives and limited removal powers. The shorter timeline means Mamdani will need to defend his education agenda to state lawmakers midway through his first term, creating an early test of his still-developing school policies.

summaries.headline: Louisiana Gets Federal Funding Flexibility Under ESSA Waiver
summaries.summary: The U.S. Department of Education approved Louisiana's request to combine state-level portions of four federal K-12 grant programs into a single flexible fund for statewide school improvement efforts. The waiver, which runs through 2029 and covers more than $18 million in federal funding, allows the state to merge allocations for teacher training, English learner services, student support programs, and extended learning activities. Louisiana becomes the second state to receive such flexibility under the Trump administration, following Iowa's similar approval in January, suggesting a pattern of federal deregulation that could reshape how states deploy targeted federal education dollars.

summaries.headline: Student Mental Health Drives More Absences Than Illness
summaries.summary: New national survey data reveals that while nearly all students miss school occasionally for illness, chronic absenteeism stems primarily from less common but high-impact factors like mental health struggles, family caregiving responsibilities, and transportation barriers. Students reporting emotional or psychological challenges miss an average of 12 more days than their peers, with some describing mornings when attendance feels impossible due to anxiety or depression. The findings suggest districts may need to shift intervention strategies from addressing routine illness to tackling these concentrated, high-impact drivers that affect fewer students but generate significantly more missed days per case.

summaries.headline: Colorado Keeps Homeschool Enrichment Funding Rate Despite Budget Pressures
summaries.summary: Colorado lawmakers preserved the current per-pupil funding rate of about $6,000 for homeschool enrichment students despite facing a $1.5 billion budget shortfall and concerns about program oversight. Instead of cutting the rate, legislators chose to eliminate some programs offered through ERBOCES, a cooperative that had authorized activities ranging from sports camps to ski passes using public dollars meant for education. The decision maintains funding for the state's $100 million part-time student program while signaling that lawmakers may revisit rate reductions as they continue wrestling with the growth and regulation of publicly funded homeschool enrichment.

summaries.headline: Connecticut Technical Schools Show Promise for Disengaged Boys
summaries.summary: Boys accepted into Connecticut's competitive technical high schools demonstrate significantly better attendance, test scores, graduation rates, and future earnings compared to peers who narrowly missed admission cutoffs, while girls see no such advantage over their rejected counterparts. Only 44 percent of the 7,850 applicants gained admission to the state's 17 technical schools this year, with overall enrollment running 70 percent male and some programs like carpentry attracting almost exclusively boys. The findings arrive as boys nationally lag behind girls across multiple academic measures, suggesting career-focused education models may offer a pathway for re-engaging male students who struggle in traditional classroom settings.

summaries.headline: Learning Decline Predates Pandemic, Causes Remain Unclear
summaries.summary: Harvard researcher Tom Kane's comprehensive analysis of national test score data reveals that U.S. students have been in a "learning recession" since around 2013, with pandemic-related losses layered on top of an existing decline. Kane identifies two possible culprits — the dismantling of test-based accountability systems and rising social media use — but acknowledges the evidence remains circumstantial, with neither theory fully explaining why reading scores have suffered more persistent declines than math. The findings suggest that recovery efforts must address deeper structural issues beyond pandemic remediation, though even leading experts lack definitive explanations for the long-term slide in student achievement.

summaries.headline: NYC PTA Fundraising Reveals Stark School Wealth Gaps
summaries.summary: New York City's top 30 schools raised nearly half of all PTA funds last year, while roughly a third of the city's 1,240 schools reported raising no money at all, according to newly released Education Department data for 2024-25. The highest-earning PTA brought in more than $3 million, creating what researchers describe as a snowball effect where well-funded schools can attract more engaged families and potentially drive up local housing prices. These disparities allow affluent schools to fund enrichment programs, teaching assistants, and staff retention efforts that less wealthy schools cannot match, potentially widening existing achievement gaps across the nation's largest school district.

summaries.headline: New York Voters Approve 96% of School Budgets
summaries.summary: New York state voters approved 96% of proposed school district budgets on Tuesday, with districts staying within property tax caps seeing even higher success rates at 98%. More than three dozen districts sought to override the 2% property tax cap, requiring a 60% supermajority for passage—25 of these 38 districts succeeded while 13 failed. The strong approval rates come as state lawmakers review an education budget bill that includes a 2% Foundation Aid increase for all districts and reforms to the funding formula, suggesting voter support remains solid even as districts navigate state funding changes.

summaries.headline: Four Johnson County Districts Sue Kansas Over Special Education Funding
summaries.summary: Four Johnson County school districts—Blue Valley, De Soto, Olathe, and Shawnee Mission—are pursuing litigation against Kansas over chronic underfunding of special education services that has persisted for 15 years. Kansas districts paid $440 million for special education last year while the state covered only 75% of required excess costs instead of the legally mandated 92%, forcing local districts to divert hundreds of millions from general funds to meet federal requirements. The coalition represents 83,000 students and signals growing willingness among well-resourced districts to challenge state funding formulas through the courts rather than continue subsidizing state obligations.

summaries.headline: Small District Builds Unified K-12 Literacy Vision
summaries.summary: Whiteville City Schools developed a comprehensive literacy strategy spanning all grade levels to address reading achievement gaps in their North Carolina district. The small district aligned instructional practices, professional development, and assessment systems around science of reading principles while maintaining flexibility for individual school needs. Their systematic approach demonstrates how smaller systems can leverage their agility to implement coherent literacy reforms that larger districts often struggle to coordinate across multiple schools and stakeholders.

summaries.headline: Google Workspace Adds Voice Drafting to Docs
summaries.summary: Google announced new AI features for Workspace users, including Docs Live for voice-based document creation and Google Pics for AI image editing, rolling out this summer to Google AI subscribers and Workspace business customers. Docs Live allows users to speak ideas while Gemini structures them into documents and pulls information from Gmail, Drive, and Chat with user permission, while Google Pics offers image generation and object-level editing capabilities. The updates reach Google's four billion Workspace users at a time when districts are still developing policies around AI tools that can access student data across multiple school platforms.

summaries.headline: Indiana Charters Outpaced Traditional Schools in Post-COVID Recovery
summaries.summary: Indiana charter school students showed greater academic growth than their traditional public school peers in the years following the pandemic, according to a preliminary analysis tracking students from 2017-18 to 2023-24. The gains were particularly pronounced for Black and Hispanic students and those who were lowest-performing and economically disadvantaged, with researchers examining ILEARN test score improvements from pandemic baseline levels in 2020-21. The findings have prompted researchers to investigate what specific recovery strategies charter leaders employed, potentially offering insights into effective approaches for addressing learning loss across all school types.

summaries.headline: Achievement Decline Began Before Pandemic Hit Schools
summaries.summary: Student achievement started dropping in 2013, years before COVID-19 disrupted education systems, according to new research examining the timeline of academic performance declines. Researchers describe the pandemic as "the mudslide" that accelerated an existing trend, with one attributing the earlier decline to increased technology integration in schools coinciding with what they term a "breakdown" in high-stakes testing systems. The findings suggest that post-pandemic recovery efforts may need to address pre-existing structural issues rather than focusing solely on making up for lost learning during school closures.

summaries.headline: Attendance Patterns Signal Students' Mental Health Needs
summaries.summary: Children with anxiety and depression are more than 3 times as likely as their peers to experience health-related school absenteeism, according to research highlighted by Dr. Michelle Shankar. The missed school time stems from multiple factors including school refusal, poor engagement, behavioral concerns, and disciplinary actions like out-of-school suspensions. Changes in attendance patterns can serve as an early warning system for families, schools, and pediatricians to identify students with underlying mental or behavioral health needs before they escalate.

summaries.headline: Camden High Leads New Jersey in Chronic Absenteeism
summaries.summary: Camden High School posted the state's worst attendance record in 2024-25, with 54% of students absent 20% or more school days and a chronic absenteeism rate of 75% — five times higher than the state average of 14.4%. Other Camden schools also struggled significantly, with Camden Prep's chronic absenteeism rate more than doubling from 32% in 2022-23 to 66.3% in 2024-25, while the district's overall attendance crisis has worsened over three consecutive years. The data underscore how attendance challenges in high-poverty urban districts can compound academic recovery efforts, particularly as the new superintendent identifies chronic absenteeism as a priority focus area.

# Why Are People Blaming The Freedom Caucus For $4 Billion School Funding Package?

People are blaming — and crediting — the Wyoming Freedom Caucus for the Legislature's nearly $4 billion school spending package. Whether the caucus deserves either depends on whom you ask, but the package had "overwhelming support" from both parties.

![](https://cowboystatedaily.imgix.net/clair-headshot-2-11-22-23.jpg?ixlib=js-3.8.0&q=75&auto=format%2Ccompress&w=100&h=100&fit=crop&ar=1%3A1)

[Clair McFarland](https://cowboystatedaily.com/author/clair-mcfarland/)

May 21, 20269 min read

![People are blaming — and crediting — the Wyoming Freedom Caucus for the Wyoming Legislature’s nearly $4 billion school spending package. Whether the caucus deserves either depends on whom you ask. It had “overwhelming support” across the Legislature. Above, Freedom Caucus members outside the state Capitol in Cheyenne during the 2026 legislative session.](https://cowboystatedaily.imgix.net/Freedom-Caucus-5.21.26.jpg?ixlib=js-3.8.0&q=75&auto=format%2Ccompress)

People are blaming — and crediting — the Wyoming Freedom Caucus for the Wyoming Legislature’s nearly $4 billion school spending package. Whether the caucus deserves either depends on whom you ask. It had “overwhelming support” across the Legislature. Above, Freedom Caucus members outside the state Capitol in Cheyenne during the 2026 legislative session. (Matt Idler for Cowboy State Daily)

People are blaming the Wyoming Freedom Caucus for the Wyoming Legislature’s nearly $4 billion per-biennium school spending package.

Whether that’s justified depends on whom you ask. So does the question of whether giving credit is more appropriate than giving blame for the court-ordered, long-overdue spending plan.

On the one hand, the Wyoming Freedom Caucus’ former chair, speaking on behalf of the caucus, [took credit for the package](https://cowboystatedaily.com/2026/04/17/guest-column-which-freedom-caucus-accomplishments-anger-you-most/ "https://cowboystatedaily.com/2026/04/17/guest-column-which-freedom-caucus-accomplishments-anger-you-most/") after it became law.

On the other hand, the spending plan itself contains a mix of favored and hated provisions, and it’s often misunderstood.

“Now, to say this was a bill that was brought forward by a small caucus — it can’t be,” said state House Majority Floor Leader Scott Heiner, R-Green River, during a virtual townhall meeting Wednesday evening. “Because it was overwhelmingly supported by all the legislators, except for seven (in the House).”

Heiner co-chairs the committee that built the first draft of the spending package: the Select Committee on School Finance Recalibration.

In Wyoming, “recalibration” refers to an arduous process in which lawmakers reevaluate what public K-12 education costs, hear consultant recommendations and public comment, and rewrite the state’s mechanism for funding public schools.

“(The package) had overwhelming support not only from the Republicans, but Democrats — and everyone in the Legislature,” Heiner added.

His assessment is correct.

## The Blame

Yet, when a Wyoming High School Activities Association (WHSAA) press release [warned of potential cuts](https://cowboystatedaily.com/2026/05/11/wyoming-schools-urged-against-hacking-and-whacking-of-school-programs-over-money/ "https://cowboystatedaily.com/2026/05/11/wyoming-schools-urged-against-hacking-and-whacking-of-school-programs-over-money/") to school activities, many in the public criticized the Freedom Caucus.

“The Freedom Caucus was able to take a deadly shot at the heart of high school activities and athletics by cutting the budget by 8.4 percent,” wrote columnist and reporter Randy Tucker in a [May 11 column](https://county10.com/the-streak-ends-here/ "https://county10.com/the-streak-ends-here/") for Fremont County-based outlet County10.

The “impending funding shortfall in activities and academics,” Tucker added, “will be disastrous and arrive very soon, just a few months from now.”

Under Casper-based Republican Rep. Elissa Cambpell’s Facebook [re-post of the WHSAA statement](https://www.facebook.com/share/p/1DVYS3YH9S/ "https://www.facebook.com/share/p/1DVYS3YH9S/"), the commenters wrote things like:

• “You voted the Freedom Caucus in, and now you’ll have a hell of a time getting them out,”

• “#freedomcaucusstealingfreedom,”

• “This catastrophe is brought to you by the voters blindly following the freeDumb caucus candidates and MAGA cult.”

Tucker told Cowboy State Daily in a Thursday phone interview that he felt comfortable blaming the caucus because its members or allies chair multiple House committees.

Heiner chairs the House side of the recalibration committee. Rep. Ocean Andrew, R-Laramie, who often votes with the caucus but told Cowboy State Daily he’s not a member, chairs the House Education Committee.

“The Freedom Caucus was pretty good at getting themselves into committee chairmanships and so forth,” said Tucker.

The columnist also cast the caucus’ uncertain membership roster, group statements, and frequent bloc voting as measures that obfuscate real debate and problem-solving.

“It’s a collective thing,” he said.

## The Credit

The caucus on March 5 issued a statement calling the recalibration bill “a win” for students and teachers, and proof that “conservatives can govern.”

“We did what the Insiders have failed to do for 15 years by passing a strong school finance bill,” says the statement.

Former caucus chair, and current member Rep. John Bear, R-Gillette, took credit on the caucus’ behalf in an April 17 [guest column for Cowboy State Daily](https://cowboystatedaily.com/2026/04/17/guest-column-which-freedom-caucus-accomplishments-anger-you-most/ "https://cowboystatedaily.com/2026/04/17/guest-column-which-freedom-caucus-accomplishments-anger-you-most/").

“We passed a historic school finance bill that locks state dollars in the classroom, providing double-digit pay increases for teachers and expanding CTE and dual enrollment opportunities for Wyoming kids,” says the column. “Who wouldn’t want to ensure tax money actually funds teachers and students?”

That was about three weeks before the WHSAA statement and other public discourse sparked outrage and fear of gutted activities – stemming from what lawmakers called bugs in the package that they intend to fix.

But, popular blame notwithstanding, Bear maintained his position in a Thursday phone interview with Cowboy State Daily.

“It’s certainly something the entire Legislature did, but we led the effort,” said Bear. “The criticisms about what is going on the bill are, you know, hyperbolic, first of all. A lot of moving parts.”

Also, Bear noted, recalibrators have pledged since January to keep researching and tweaking the package in the coming months, to address additional funding requirements a court ordered in 2025.

This year’s recalibration package is the largest in Wyoming history, Heiner said during the Wednesday townhall.

Bear said the caucus has stayed mindful of its conservative principles, but still had an obligation to help build the spending plan. Law requires the Legislature recalibrate K-12 funding at least every five years. Until March, it hadn’t done it in at least 15 years.

The new funding model increases K-12 money for the coming school year by about by approximately $114.1 million, or 8.6%. That equates to about $1.95 billion per school year or nearly $4 billion per biennium - and about $22,626 per-student, per year.

The state is increasing its recommended salaries for teachers by an estimated 20.7%. It's adding about 260 teacher positions.

“It’s about leadership, when it comes to getting things accomplished,” Bear said.

## The Facts

Three of the 12 members of the recalibration committee, including Heiner, are also known members of the Wyoming Freedom Caucus – a controversial and conservative group of House Republicans.

Two Democrats and 10 Republicans serve on the committee altogether.

All 12 members voted in January to advance the recalibration package.

The [House killed it](https://cowboystatedaily.com/2026/02/09/wyoming-house-kills-bill-to-change-how-schools-get-money-senate-could-save-it/ "https://cowboystatedaily.com/2026/02/09/wyoming-house-kills-bill-to-change-how-schools-get-money-senate-could-save-it/") Feb. 9, by voting 41-21 in favor of its introduction. That’s one vote shy of the two-thirds threshold required to introduce non-budget bills in even-numbered years.

The state Senate [rescued the package](https://cowboystatedaily.com/2026/02/13/senate-rescues-wyomings-attempt-to-rework-public-school-funding/ "https://cowboystatedaily.com/2026/02/13/senate-rescues-wyomings-attempt-to-rework-public-school-funding/") with a unanimous introductory vote four days later.

Sen. Chris Rothfuss, D-Laramie, a key architect of the package, [added both extra dollars and extra accountability measures](https://cowboystatedaily.com/2026/02/16/wyoming-senator-offers-126-million-compromise-to-embattled-school-funding-bill/ "https://cowboystatedaily.com/2026/02/16/wyoming-senator-offers-126-million-compromise-to-embattled-school-funding-bill/") to the package during a Senate Education Committee the following week.

The Senate voted 30-1 to send the package to the House, which generally kept Rothfuss’ changes and passed the bill 52-7.

The seven nay-votes came from non-Freedom Caucus Republicans. The five chamber Democrats who were present (out of six total in the House) voted aye.

Rather than veto or sign the package, Gov. Mark Gordon let it become law [without his signature](https://cowboystatedaily.com/2026/03/09/nearly-4-billion-wyoming-education-plan-goes-into-law-without-gordons-signature/ "https://cowboystatedaily.com/2026/03/09/nearly-4-billion-wyoming-education-plan-goes-into-law-without-gordons-signature/").

Money for school sports and activities is now expected to drop from $46.3 million to $42.4 million per school year.

Dropping enrollment is a factor driving that.

So too is the educational “silo.” That’s a provision banning districts from using money for classroom educators in other areas, like equipment, administration – or activities.

It follows what some recalibrators have described as a decade of complaints, that districts can’t pay and hire teachers well enough.

House Speaker Chip Neiman, R-Hulett, told Cowboy State Daily the state has seen too many dollars meant to address those complaints go “sideways” into other areas. The silo is exposing more of those maneuvers, and has brought compliments from many teachers, he added.

The Wyoming Education Association sued the state over K-12 funding shortages, and the judge who ordered better funding said the schools had shown their educators are underfunded.

"Why you spending so much on activities?" asked Neiman in a Thursday rhetorical. "If you don’t have enough money to hire teachers; then put the money there."

The silo was response to "getting sued and losing," as well as the prevailing concerns of the past several years, he added.

## Everybody Calm Down

Rep. Tom Kelly, R-Sheridan, often votes with the Freedom Caucus, but has said he’s not a member of it and has [contradicted caucus members on some efforts](https://cowboystatedaily.com/2025/02/07/wyoming-committee-kills-sweeping-and-almost-vindictive-anti-obscenity-law/ "https://cowboystatedaily.com/2025/02/07/wyoming-committee-kills-sweeping-and-almost-vindictive-anti-obscenity-law/").

He’s also a member of the recalibration committee.

Kelly took to Facebook May 15 to address the “consternation” around the drop in activities funding, and to attribute the drop to declining enrollment – since activities are funded on a per-student basis.

Heiner told Cowboy State Daily earlier this month that, while enrollment is a factor, the state also adopted its consultant’s new formula for activities funding, and intends to reevaluate that formula the coming months.

Kelly’s statement continues: “As far as a public announcement warning that school activities are about to be cut, that is a political tactic that I don’t really like.”

He said he saw similar tactics in Illinois, geared toward taking policy hiccups “out on the kids” to “start a public uproar rather than start a productive conversation.”

In the meantime, Heiner and Neiman have all urged the districts to tap into their reserves as necessary – some of which are sizable – while lawmakers address activities funding in the coming months.

Rothfuss has also pledged to address the issue in the coming months.

As for whose credit or blame the spending package tallies, Rothfuss said lawmakers should focus less on taking credit, and more on “just trying to help people.”

## Wait, What?

While the activities money and the teacher silo have met with controversy, three mental health groups say some districts are responding altogether contrary to the package’s mission.

The Wyoming Behavioral Health Alliance and its members the Wyoming Counseling Association and Wyoming School Counseling Association dispatched a joint press release Tuesday, voicing “deep” concern over “reports across the state that some Wyoming school districts are using recalibration changes as justification for reducing or eliminating school counselor positions.”

The package, however, increased money for school counselors in every grade group.

“For the first time in Wyoming history, the Legislature specifically recognized the critical role of school counseling and funded positions adequately, including positions at the elementary level in addition to continued support across secondary levels,” says the statement. “The bill reflects a clear legislative acknowledgment that student mental health, prevention services, academic planning, and social-emotional support are essential components of a complete and uniform public education system.”

The groups concluded by urging districts and educational leaders to preserve those jobs, and implement the bill “as intended.”

# Opinion: Alaska needs to recalibrate its school funding before communities break

By Suzanne LaFrance and Grier Hopkins

Published: May 17, 2026

![](https://www.adn.com/resizer/v2/6DFGNMXTANBWRAOXCQ4ISCVLP4.jpg?auth=3d04ddaa0c5e894ce797543d76fd28375365e9163da3ebe4619991bc5912a7f9&width=800&height=452)(iStock / Getty Images)

As the mayors of two of Alaska’s largest municipal regions, we represent more than half of the state’s population, including its two largest cities, spanning from the Fairbanks North Star Borough to the Municipality of Anchorage. While our communities are geographically and economically distinct, we are currently united by a single, urgent crisis: The state’s primary education funding formula is shifting costs onto local property taxpayers in a way that is no longer sustainable.

The partnership between the state of Alaska and local communities to fund K-12 education is frayed. Under current law, as property values rise, the state allocates less money to local school districts. This shifts costs onto local taxpayers through the required local contribution, or RLC, disincentivizes economic growth and eats away at support for local students. Because the formula subtracts this local contribution from state aid dollar-for-dollar, many communities are left running just to stand still. Even when the Legislature increases the Base Student Allocation, or BSA, property values often rise faster, perversely leaving school districts with less state funding. Local taxpayers are forced to fill the gap.

[Senate Bill 278](https://www.akleg.gov/basis/Bill/Detail/34?Root=SB%20278 "https://www.akleg.gov/basis/Bill/Detail/34?Root=SB%20278"), sponsored by Sen. Jesse Bjorkman through the Senate Education Committee, offers a commonsense, cross-partisan solution to restore fairness and predictability to this system by capping annual RLC increases at 2%.

A cross-partisan and cross-caucus vote on the floor of the Alaska State House rolled this important legislation into [House Bill 261](https://www.akleg.gov/basis/Bill/Detail/34?Root=hb261 "https://www.akleg.gov/basis/Bill/Detail/34?Root=hb261") by Rep. Andi Story. The bill then [passed the House](https://www.adn.com/politics/alaska-legislature/2026/05/12/alaska-house-passes-bill-adding-more-than-140-million-to-education-budget/ "https://www.adn.com/politics/alaska-legislature/2026/05/12/alaska-house-passes-bill-adding-more-than-140-million-to-education-budget/") in a 31-9 vote. HB 261 aims to stabilize school district funding through a smart update of the student count process by averaging the previous three years’ counts, preventing dramatic drops. The integration of SB 278 into HB 261 represents a targeted modernization of Alaska’s education funding framework, replacing a volatile and outdated formula with a predictable state-local partnership that ensures resources reach the classroom rather than being lost to municipal budget crises.

We are encouraged by the cross-partisan collaboration in the capitol that prioritizes Alaska’s students over political divisions.

### The view from our communities

In Anchorage, the problem is reaching a breaking point because of our municipal tax cap. In fiscal year 2027, Anchorage’s RLC will increase by a staggering $11.2 million. Because property taxes are capped, we cannot simply “find” that money. Fulfilling this state mandate could force us to cut essential services — meaning fewer police officers on the street, slower fire response times or deferred maintenance on our roads. It also makes it harder to contribute more to schools under our allowable maximum local contribution.

In Fairbanks, the required local effort has climbed by nearly $3.4 million over three years. The state’s “full value determination” often overstates a community’s actual ability to pay, counting targeted exemptions created locally to incentivize economic development and new housing that aren’t practically available to generate revenue. Additionally, the local tax cap does not bring in new revenue with increased assessments, making the RLC a double hit to Interior residents.

ADVERTISEMENT

Critically, SB 278 is not about the state “giving” more money to districts. It is about the state taking less from local taxpayers to fulfill its own constitutional duty. By modernizing this formula, the state ensures that education funding remains a stable partnership rather than a volatile hidden tax on local taxpayers and communities.

We recognize that broader reform is still needed, including a meaningful increase to the BSA and addressing equity for our rural and REAA districts. However, we cannot let the search for “perfect” prevent us from solving an immediate crisis.

Across the state, we are hearing devastating stories of exponential class size growth, school closures and the loss of treasured programs. We cannot afford to wait for a multiyear study while our districts are hemorrhaging staff today.

SB 278 has earned the support of the Alaska Municipal League and leaders across the political spectrum because it respects local control and provides the predictability our taxpayers deserve. It is a vital step toward a sustainable future for our students.

ADVERTISEMENT

We urge the Alaska State Legislature to pass SB 278. Let’s restore the balance in our state-local partnership and ensure that our schools — and our communities — can thrive.

_**Suzanne LaFrance**_ _is the mayor of the Municipality of Anchorage. LaFrance served two terms on the Anchorage Assembly, including two years as chair._

_**Grier Hopkins**_ _is the mayor of the Fairbanks North Star Borough. Hopkins served in the Alaska State House from 2018 to 2022._

# Commissioner Moyer proposes to restore all SUN School Funding.

Offered by

- [Commissioner Moyer](https://multco.us/taxonomy/term/214)

May 20, 2026

## The budget amendment fully restores SUN Community Schools by reducing  internal administrative and support services countywide.

Multnomah County Commissioner Meghan Moyer introduced a budget amendment to restore funding to SUN Community Schools, which is slated to eliminate 9 sites in the Chair’s Proposed Budget. The $1.2m funding restoration maintains current

funding levels by reducing Multnomah County’s internal administrative and support infrastructure. Moyer’s budget amendment, if approved, would continue County funding to 92 SUN Community School sites.

This budget amendment reflects Commissioner Moyer’s commitment to shrinking

Multnomah County’s administrative footprint to meet its fiscal reality. Multnomah County Board of Commissioners were presented with county revenue projections that foresee budget cuts over next few years primarily due to inflationary pressures and the loss of federal & state funding. Bracing for revenue shortfalls in this budget year and beyond, Commissioner Moyer is pushing for leaner county administration in order to preserve services for Multnomah County residents.

Schools Uniting Neighborhoods (SUN) Community Schools play a vital role in strengthening school communities by connecting students to after school programs, academic support and summer learning opportunities. Multnomah County contracts with community-based organizations to provide culturally responsive services to students, as well as, support their families through engagement, community resource connections and social emotional services. If the budget amendment does not pass, the nine site closures would disproportionately impact low-income families, working parents and students of color who rely on these services — especially for families experiencing fear and uncertainty related to immigration enforcement.

“In meeting our fiscal reality, it is my belief that the County shoulders as much of the pain of budget cuts as possible in order to maintain community services,” said

Commissioner Moyer.

The Wisconsin Senate last week struck down a bill that would have cut property and income taxes and allocated millions of dollars to public schools, despite Gov. **Tony Evers**’ stamp of approval.

Among other things, the legislation would have approved $300 million for special education funding and another $300 million for school general aids, while providing around $50 million in tax relief through provisions that would reimburse taxpayers and eliminate taxes on tips and overtime.

While it is marketing in the end, the effort does make me chuckle.

Like many of you, I get marketing emails — you can control most of the flow, but not all.

One of them that feels ironic emanates from Experian. It’s along the lines of, “Congratulations. You have new credit card matches.”

When in actuality, it should likely state, “Congratulations. You have the opportunity to accumulate more debt. So instead of paying down debt and living within your means, we want you to be more indebted.”

It’s easy to spend someone else’s money.

We all do it. But some are more blatant than others.

As we wind down another school year, one of the last things in the world I want to bring up in this space is anything attached to school funding.

On your social-media feeds. In your communities. Everyone’s seemingly an expert on what to do about this obvious problem in Ohio.

Districts are cutting. Levies are proposed. A bleak future without changes is outlined.

Daring to broach the subject on, say, Facebook is mission impossible. Because there are certain topics, even when addressed lightly, that lead to those Facebook friends — who wouldn’t react to anything else from personal triumph to tragedy — but will pounce in those comments to argue.

In other words, there is enough debate to go around on school funding.

Far be it for me to “go there.” You don’t want to hear it here. You don’t want to argue it here. Neither do I.

However, with that noted, that aforementioned bleak future with funding does have an effect on the facet that unites us here: High school sports.

No, when the No. 1 priority of a school or school district is to educate children, high school sports in and of itself isn’t the primary consideration. Ever.

But, as this topic becomes louder and more frequent, we do have to ask ourselves:

When do we begin to start worrying about a lack of funding having a catastrophic impact on high school sports? And no, by the way, the word “catastrophic” is not reaching.

While asking that all-too-vital question as well, it is natural to also ponder, “Just how much does that matter if sports can be or cannot be funded?”

Please, again, I’m not trying to get into a debate on school funding. Have your opinions. Argue with others and refine them in due course toward a solution.

But if available funds must be applied to education and high school sports — middle school sports, too, obviously — is not a priority in comparison, sports budgets are a place that can and will be cut.

You hear it all the time when levies go on the ballot, as they have this year.

A school district will head to its residents seeking sustained or more funds.

It will lay out how the money would be spent.

It will also lay out what cuts would be made if it’s not available.

The aspects that get cut or are adjusted do not vary that much.

Freshman and junior varsity. So-called “niche sports” might face the proverbial ax.

Fewer coaches. No money for new equipment or facility upgrades.

Not to mention the one adjustment that makes everyone involved cringe: The introduction of or increase to “pay to play.”

There are districts right now in our coverage area facing pay to play well into the triple digits, if not four figures per student. Those costs, as well as the amount of schools who will have to ask, will only grow as the school funding impasse grows.

Some families can afford it. Some student-athletes can make it happen through jobs or fundraising. Some districts are fortunate enough to have generous local businesses or residents/alumni who act as underwriters so competition can continue. But not all.

Dips in participation. Not enough resources to field teams.

If the money isn’t there, that’s what happens.

No one prefers it, of course. But that’s what happens.

Under that scenario, as it normally does, the power will rest even more with the haves vs. the have nots. Is that fair? Right? Society in action?

Whatever the answers are, it’s going to be more prevalent if there’s less money or none at all.

It’s natural, I think, for all of us to play backseat logistics manager or chief financial officer from time to time.

When you see a bus drop off student-athletes at an event, say, 30 miles away, and then they head back to campus without other scheduled stops but then head back to pick them up after the event, you do wonder if gas and transportation could be spared to some extent just staying there and not doing the 60 extra miles round-trip.

When you see conferences of neighboring, similar-sized schools unable to stay together and having to opt for conferences with longer miles and longer days and nights, you do wonder if it’s worth the tradeoff.

When you see new uniforms or new upgrades, you do wonder if it could have waited a year.

But on the other side, the people dispersing these funds and managing budgets are facing the same conundrums. And headaches.

It’s impossible not to go there, so to speak: Will it ever get so bad with not having resources that schools, rightly needing to focus on the academic component of their mission, just can’t offer some or all sports or extracurriculars?

And if they can’t, how consequential is that?

The last thing along these lines anyone wants — and I couldn’t care less if or how you argue the point of school funding — is to begin seeing stories about high school sports taking body blows toward elimination.

Seemingly, however, that’s where we are.

So hopefully, people a lot smarter and more powerful than me can figure this out.

Because high school sports are on the line here.

How much? Here’s to hoping we never find out.

# Local voters decide on millions’ worth of school funding

Local voters decided on millions of dollars worth of school funding on Tuesday.

Several Idaho school districts across the region pitched ballot measures during the primary election. All levies were passing as of Tuesday night; however, results are subject to change as county auditors continue to count votes.

It appears that Nez Perce and Lewis counties’ supplemental levy for Culdesac School District is passing by 64%. The measure received 135 votes in favor of and 74 votes against in Nez Perce, and four votes for and three votes against in Lewis.

Culdesac’s $250,000 two-year request would finance building maintenance, insurance, technology, supplies and student activities. The tax per $100,000 of assessed home value will remain the same at $243.18 if passed.

Highland School District’s two-year $599,000 levy looks to be passing with a 61% approval rate. The multi-county contest received 239 votes in favor of and 157 votes in opposition to the measure in Lewis County. In Nez Perce County, 33 votes were placed for and 14 votes were made against it. Idaho County voters cast two yes votes and two no votes.

The request may fund career technical education, half-day kindergarten, staff salaries, classroom resources, busing and athletics. This will not change the tax per $100,000 of assessed value of $253.49.

Nezperce School District’s $445,000 levy for one year, appears to be passing by 69%. Lewis County residents cast 186 yes votes to 83 no votes. Idaho County cast 21 approving votes to 12 disapproving. Clearwater County cast seven votes in favor of and three votes in opposition.

Salaries, security, technology, maintenance, transportation, athletics and curriculum would be funded by the request. If passed, the measure would lower the tax per $100,000 of assessed value from $256.13 to $253.82.

Potlatch School District’s $1,650,000 ask for one year is narrowly passing by 53%. Latah County constituents are split between 558 votes approving and 498 votes denying the levy.

The measure would finance career and technical programs, extracurricular activities, building maintenance, and special education staff. If passed, the cost is expected to be $336.67 per $100,000 of taxable assessed value.

The $275,000 one-year levy from Cottonwood School District was passing by 68% Tuesday night. The request received 313 votes for and 150 votes against in Idaho County. Lewis County did not publish results by press time.

Technology, utilities, substitute teachers, maintenance, food services and speech and language services would be supported by the measure. If passed, the tax per $100,000 of assessed value would be an estimated $89.91.

Salmon River School District’s $525,000 levy for one year is passing by 58%. In Idaho County, the measure received 138 yes votes to 79 no votes. Adams County constituents cast 22 votes in favor of and four against it. The request would fund staff salaries and extracurricular services. The proposed tax would be $148.69 per $100,000 of assessed value.

Grangeville School District’s one-year $805,000 levy appears to be passing by 59% in Idaho County with 1,250 votes in favor of an 880 against the measure.

Extracurricular activities, staffing and library services would be supported if passed. The measure would lower the tax per $100,000 of assessed value from $182.16 to $83.67 if approved.

Jim Herrin \| Herald-Citizen

One of the candidates running for a seat on the county commission in the August general election took advantage of the public comment period during this month's county commission meeting to advocate for additional money to support the school system.

Trenton Strode, who is the Democratic candidate in District 11, spoke as commissioners considered approving budget amendments for the school system.

"Over the past few weeks, we've heard about the projected $5.1 million shortfall facing the Putnam County school system," he said. "We've heard about inflation, insurance increases, maintenance costs, staffing concerns and federal funding drying up."

Strode said those issues were "not just a county problem."

"This is a state leadership problem," he said. "While counties like Putnam are trying to figure out how to keep our schools stable, too much of the conversation that's coming out of Nashville currently has been based on political theatre and national culture war issues — instead of the real financial pressures that our local government is dealing with."

Strode urged the commission to pass a resolution calling for the legislature to provide additional school funding.

"The commission has passed resolutions before when some things matter to Putnam County, and so I challenge this body to begin drafting and pursuing resolutions to the state legislature, demanding stronger, long-term public school funding protections," he said. "I also encourage this commission to seriously consider funding the full $5.1 million shortfall facing our school system."

He added, "If we can speak up on national symbolic political issues like the Second Amendment and sanctuary cities, then surely we can speak up for our teachers, our schools, our students and our taxpayers."

He said the funding being requested by the school system in the coming year is an "investment \[in\] the future workforce of this county."

"It's not a luxury expense," he said.

Strode is one of four candidates who will be on the ballot in District 11. The others are Republicans Darren Wilson and Kathy Dunn and Independent candidate Marsha Kay Bowman.
